card.title: Leaf
card.summary: Portfolio project for the Google UX Design Certificate. Full UX process with a real usability study (SUS 76).

hero.title: Leaf
hero.tagline: Care for your plants without guessing when to water them.

problem.heading: A visual and functional language for daily care.
problem.body: Leaf was born as the capstone for my Google UX Design Certificate: an app that helps indoor-plant owners organize watering, light, and general-care reminders. The challenge wasn't technical — it was finding the right tone: useful without being controlling, calm without being boring.

research.heading: I started by listening.
research.body: I designed three personas, ran a competitive audit, defined the value proposition, and framed 'How Might We…' questions and goal statements for each. Research surfaced two common failure modes across the category: asking users for too much upfront, or turning plant care into an anxious to-do list. Leaf had to do the opposite.
bullets: Personas grounded in 5 real user interviews, March 2025.
Competitive audit across 4 apps — Greg, Planta, PictureThis, and Google Lens.
Value proposition built around four categories: simplicity, personalization, accuracy, efficiency.
Goal statements and 'How Might We…' questions, one set per persona.

personas.name: Sofia Ramirez, 27
personas.role: UX Researcher, Brooklyn, NY — first-time plant owner with five plants and zero prior experience, learning from apps and YouTube.
personas.goals: Understand what each plant needs without doing research · get simple, timely reminders before it's too late · build confidence as a new plant owner.
personas.frustrations: Apps use terms she doesn't understand · photo ID fails on first tries, breaking trust immediately · basic features are locked behind a subscription.
personas.statement: Sofia is a first-time plant owner who needs an app that meets her where she is — not where an expert would be — because every time an app assumes she already knows what 'well-draining soil' means, it confirms her fear that plant care is too complicated for someone like her.

personas.name: Carlos Mendez, 38
personas.role: Accountant, Los Angeles, CA — twelve plants and an inconsistent routine, travels often for work.
personas.goals: Never over- or under-water a plant again · trust that his data is always safe and synced · log care in one tap without digging through menus.
personas.frustrations: Lost a year of plant data after a phone update, with no recovery path · can't easily customize watering per plant · notifications mix care alerts with marketing.
personas.statement: Carlos is a busy professional who needs an app that works with his life instead of against it — remembering his plants, his schedule, and his preferences — because right now the app demands more from him than his plants do.

personas.name: Mayelin Perez, 52
personas.role: Commerce Specialist, Cuba — 20+ plants and decades of experience, monitors soil humidity daily; internet access is unreliable.
personas.goals: Access her full plant library and care history at any time · get environment-specific recommendations without internet · sync automatically once a connection returns.
personas.frustrations: The app fails completely without an internet connection · generic recommendations ignore her real climate and plants · no way to enter her actual environment or watering method.
personas.statement: Mayelin is an experienced plant owner who needs a plant care app that works reliably without internet access — because where she lives, connectivity is inconsistent, and an app that stops working the moment the signal drops isn't a tool she can trust.

research.insight: The real problem wasn't a lack of information — every competitor already floods people with care tips. It was a lack of relevance: no app adapted to who you actually are, where you live, or how much you already know. A first-timer, a forgetful professional, and a 20-year expert with no reliable internet were all being handed the exact same advice.

figure.label: Storyboard — Mayelin Perez
figure.caption: One of three hand-drawn storyboards from the empathize phase. Mayelin's plant is stressed and her app won't load with no connection — until she finds one that works fully offline, no exception.

process.heading: From wireframes to a design system.
process.body: Every screen started on paper before it touched Figma — fast, disposable sketches to test layout logic before committing to pixels. Low-fidelity digital wireframes came next, iterated on before any color or typography entered the picture. The design system is built in layers: primitives with 10-step tonal ramps — forest green (#2D5016) over warm beige, with amber, blue, and red accents —, a semantic layer mapping each primitive to its role (background, text, borders, statuses) ready for light and dark modes, and Inter as the app's single typeface. Every ReminderCard, button, and bottom-sheet overlay lives as a Figma component, and the high-fidelity build moved to development with Claude Code via MCP.

figure.label: Value proposition
figure.caption: The full working canvas, start to finish: every feature idea, sorted into four categories, each one traced back to the real participant who needed it, then checked against what competitors already offer. It ends in a single line — "The app that stops giving everyone the same advice." Scroll to see the whole thing.

flows: Home — next care at a glance

flowGroups.title: Onboarding & first run
flows: First run — scan your first plant
notes: One full-bleed photo and a single primary CTA: the first screen sells calm, not a feature list.
Onboarding shows the real identify screen to set expectations before asking for anything.
‘Continue as Guest’ lowers signup friction — you can try the app before creating an account.
The first step is concrete —scan a plant— instead of an empty state that doesn't say what to do.

flowGroups.title: The app in use
flows: Home — next care at a glance
notes: Home prioritizes ‘next care’ over full inventory — a direct change from the usability study.
A green banner sums up ‘3 plants need water today’: the urgent action sits right at the top.
A quick-action row (Water, Schedule, Diagnose, Notes) over a legible care table.
One big action —‘Water Now’— with the context of when it was last watered.
The schedule splits pending and done, with ‘2 of 6’ progress to give a sense of momentum.
Framing brackets guide the shot: the user knows exactly where to point.
Suggestion chips (‘Identify a plant’, ‘Watering tips’) break the blank-input barrier.

testing.heading: Testing before calling it done.
testing.body: Five participants completed the same 5 tasks — independently, unmoderated, on a low-fidelity Figma prototype: identify a plant by camera, review its diagnosis, set a watering reminder, find the notes page, and locate upcoming reminders back on the homepage.

findings.title: Bottom navigation icons need labels
findings.quote: I'm mostly guessing what these icons mean.
findings.recommendation: Add text labels under every bottom-nav icon. Navigation was the only task where all 5 participants ran into some difficulty, usually tapping the wrong tab first.

findings.title: The identify button doesn't stand out enough
findings.quote: The camera feature could stand out more.
findings.recommendation: Strengthen the visual hierarchy of the scan CTA on the homepage so it reads as the obvious first move, not something users have to scan the page to find.

testing.insight: Every participant finished every task — Leaf wasn't hard to use, it was hard to feel sure about. Icons with no labels and a diagnosis that didn't explain itself made people doubt choices they'd already gotten right.

results.heading: A good score, backed by real testing.
results.body: The same study that surfaced the navigation and confidence issues above also included a System Usability Scale survey. The final score was 76 — above the industry average (68), squarely in the 'good' range.
learnings: Users wanted to see at a glance which plant needed attention today — I redesigned the home to prioritize 'next care' over full inventory.
Onboarding asked for too much upfront — I broke it into progressive steps with an option to defer detail.
Reminder copy worked better concise and warm-toned, not like a system notification.

reflection.heading: What I take away.
reflection.body: A good design system isn't about having many components — it's about having the right ones and using them consistently. And user research doesn't stop when design starts; it comes back to you on every iteration.

moments.title: Betting on offline-first before anyone asked for it directly
moments.body: Mayelin's interview surfaced something no competitor addresses: an app that stops working the moment the signal drops. Instead of treating offline as a fallback, I flipped the architecture — store everything locally first, sync to the cloud when a connection exists, not the other way around.

moments.title: Designing for trust, not just accuracy
moments.body: One competitor gave the same plant two different names in the same session. Another participant's plant got worse after following in-app advice. Trust breaks in one bad moment and doesn't come back — so every identification shows a confidence score, and every recommendation comes with a plain explanation of why.
